https://okcfox.com/news/local/ou-led-stu.text: New research co-authored by an Oklahoma Museum of Natural History curator and her graduate student is offering fresh insight into how animals adapt to environmental change and why protecting genetic diversity in wildlife populations could be key to surviving what comes next. The study was led by Marcos da Cruz, a University of Oklahoma Ph.D. student in the laboratory of Dr. Hayley Lanier. Lanier, the associate curator of mammals at the Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, co-authored the research alongside an international team of collaborators from the Czech Academy of Sciences. Researchers found that much of the genetic variation animals use to adapt to new environments was inherited from distant ancestors, rather than being newly evolved in response to changing conditions. “Our study helps to show that the genes underlying climate adaptation are almost entirely dependent on retained ancestral variation, not newly evolved adaptations,” Lanier said. “The size of an animal's ancestral population helps shape the amount of genetic diversity it carries today, and that diversity provides the raw material natural selection can work with as environments change.” The team focused on the bank vole, a rodent native to Europe that thrives across a broad geographic range and lives in a variety of habitats. By sequencing the entire genome of individual animals and comparing populations from different climates, the researchers identified genetic variations associated with climate adaptation and traced where those variations came from. “It supports the idea that the past history of a population is critical for shaping future responses to climate change,” Lanier said. “The more we can do to help populations retain their genetic variation—by protecting habitats and preventing population declines—the better prepared they’ll be to adapt to future environmental challenges.” Lanier described genetically diverse populations as having something like an evolutionary “tool kit,” with a larger gene pool providing more options for future generations as conditions change. “Populations that come from large, genetically diverse ancestral populations have a much broader set of genetic variations that natural selection can draw upon,” she said. “If that diversity is lost through population declines or habitat fragmentation, species may have fewer options available as they face future environmental changes.”

https://www.dw.com/en/police-exhume-body.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5KPEk Some historians believe Jan Masaryk, seen as a pro-Western figure, may have been killed by Soviet agents Image: AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Czech police said Wednesday they had begun exhuming the remains of former Czechoslovak Foreign Minister Jan Masaryk in an attempt to clear up speculation surrounding his death nearly 80 years ago. In a statement posted to X, police said they planned to examine the remains, buried at Prague 's Olsany Cemetery, "using the most modern forensic methods." "We believe that today's actions will bring us closer to clarifying the circumstances leading to the death of Jan Masaryk," the statement said. What happened to the former top diplomat? Masaryk was found dead on March 10, 1948, dressed only in his pajamas, in the courtyard at the Foreign Ministry beneath his bathroom window. The mysterious circumstances surrounding his death, at the height of the Cold War , have fueled speculation for decades. At the time, the Interior Ministry claimed that he had committed suicide. Others believed his fall may have been an accident, or that he was murdered by Soviet agents. Jan Masaryk was found in the courtyard of the Foreign Ministy, housed in Prague's Czernin Palace Image: UPI/dpa/picture-alliance Who was Jan Masaryk? Born in Prague on September 14, 1886, Masaryk was the son of the first Czechoslovak president, Tomas Garrigue Masaryk. He served as the country's top diplomat from 1940 to 1948, first for the government-in-exile during World War II and then for the post-war coalition government. Following the Czechoslovak communist coup of February 1948, he stayed on as foreign minister, refusing to step down. The case of his death has been reviewed several times since the collapse of communism in the 1989 Velvet Revolution. The country later split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia . Photograph: Ellen Schmidt/AP View image in fullscreen Police respond to a shooting Wednesday on 2 September in downtown Minneapolis. Photograph: Ellen Schmidt/AP Minneapolis Suspect and two victims dead at apartment shooting in downtown Minneapolis The city’s police department and mayor warn the public to stay away from the Loring Park neighborhood nearby Uwa Ede-Osifo Wed 2 Sep 2026 18.40 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 21.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two people were killed and the suspect was dead after a shooting at an apartment building in downtown Minneapolis on Wednesday afternoon, officials said. One shooting victim died at the scene. A second died after arriving at Hennepin county medical center, a hospital spokesperson said. Gunfire erupted on the upper floor of a high-rise apartment building, according to city officials. Video posted to social media showed police aiming rifles upward at an apartment tower near the Minneapolis convention center. After receiving several 911 calls, officers entered the building at about 4.39pm. They followed the sound of shots and encountered a “haze”, which limited their sight, officials said. Two officers were wounded by the gunfire, with one sustaining a non-life-threatening injury to the leg and a second undergoing surgery. Authorities have not publicly identified the suspect. Julius Bailey was sitting outside his apartment building when he heard gunshots and saw a man he recognized as a resident of the building holding a pistol. Bailey said he heard a woman screaming and immediately started running away. He said he counted eight shots. Bailey said he recognized the man holding the gun because he was someone who was known for showing off his weapon. Bailey said he had tried to avoid the man since moving into the building in June. “I could tell he was trouble,” he said. Chris Miller, who also lives in the apartment building, said he heard a rapid succession of gunshots and quickly ran outside for safety. He said he believed he knew who carried out the shooting and that he encountered someone in the hallway with a handgun earlier this week and reported that person to management. The Minneapolis police department and mayor Jacob Frey warned the public to stay away from the densely populated Loring Park neighborhood nearby. “Grateful to law enforcement actively working to ensure the safety of our neighbors in Downtown Minneapolis this afternoon,” Minnesota governor Tim Walz said in a statement. “Minnesota is praying for our first responders.” The FBI has extended its resources to aid law enforcement on the ground, director Kash Patel wrote in an X post.
